title: Having a go at something new
keyIdea: Having a go means trying something new or tricky, like a new food, a climbing frame or painting, even when it feels a bit scary. Big things get easier in small steps. Oops moments are part of learning, so we say "I'll have another go". New things that are hot, sharp or near a road need a grown-up first.

kid: New things can feel a bit scary. A new food. A big slide. A messy paint pot. Being brave means you try anyway. You say, "I'll have a go!"
Big things are easier in small steps. Climb one step, then the next. If you feel wobbly, stop. Take a big breath. Then try one more step.
Oops is OK. Paint drips. Towers fall down. That does not mean you are bad at it. It means you are learning. Say, "Oops! I'll have another go."
Some new things are not for trying on your own. Hot ovens, sharp knives and roads can hurt. Ask a grown-up first.
adult: Development Matters (2023) puts 'having a go' in the Characteristics of Effective Learning. In playing and exploring, children are willing to have a go. In active learning, they keep on trying when things are difficult. For 3 and 4 year olds it also expects more confidence in new situations, and choosing activities with help when needed.

Willingness to try grows from small successes. Psychologists call this self-efficacy. It also grows when adults treat mistakes as part of learning, not as proof of being 'bad at it'. Praise the trying and the strategy ('you went one step at a time') more than the result. Short, safe challenges build that confidence: a new climbing frame, new paint, a new food.

Common mistakes: rushing a child straight to the hardest part, praising only success, and treating a refusal as final. A new food often needs ten or more calm tries before a child accepts it. Looking, smelling and touching all count as steps. Be careful that 'be brave' never covers real hazards: hot, sharp and road things still need an adult first.

In the lab your child sorts new things into 'have a go' and 'ask a grown-up first'. They climb a frame one rung at a time, with a breath when it wobbles. They answer three oops moments with 'I'll have another go', take tasting steps with a new food, and fill a bear's brave meter with have-a-go words.

familyTip: Name one new thing each day and try just the first small step together: look at a new fruit, touch the bottom rung, dip one finger in the paint. When something goes wrong, say "Oops! Another go" out loud yourself so your child hears it.

practice.prompt: Your tower falls down. What can you say?
practice.hint: Does one fall mean you cannot do it?
practice.explain: Falling towers are how we learn to build. Saying "I'll have another go" helps you try again.

practice.prompt: The climbing frame has 5 steps. Ben has climbed {n} steps. How many more steps to the top?
practice.hint: Count on from {n} up to 5, one step at a time.
practice.explain: From {n} up to 5 is {=5-n} more steps. One step at a time gets Ben there.

practice.prompt: Which new thing do you ask a grown-up about first?
practice.explain: A sharp knife can cut you, so ask a grown-up first. A new song and a new puzzle are safe to try.

practice.prompt: There are {n} new fruits on the plate. Leo has a go at a tiny bite of each one. How many new fruits does he try?
practice.hint: He tries every fruit once. Count the fruits.
practice.explain: There are {n} fruits and he tries each one, so he tries {n} new fruits. Brave Leo!

pool.prompt: The big slide feels scary. What helps?
choices: A big breath, then one small step
Run to the top really fast
pool.hint: Big things are easier in small steps.
pool.explain: A breath calms the wobbly feeling. Then one small step at a time gets you up.

pool.prompt: Your paint drips on your picture. What does that mean?
pool.explain: Everyone drips when they paint. It is part of learning, so have another go.

pool.prompt: Sam tried to kick the ball {n} times and missed. Then he tried once more and scored. How many tries in all?
pool.hint: Count the misses, then add the try that scored.
pool.explain: {n} misses and 1 goal make {=n+1} tries. Sam kept having a go.

pool.prompt: A new food is on your plate. What is a good first step?
choices: Look at it and smell it
pool.hint: Tiny steps make new things less scary.
pool.explain: Looking and smelling are real steps. Touching, licking and a tiny bite can come next.

pool.prompt: Which words help you have a go?
choices: Only big kids can do it
pool.hint: Which words leave room to try again?
pool.explain: "Yet" means you are still learning. The other words stop you before you start.

pool.prompt: Which one is fine to have a go at by yourself?
pool.explain: A jigsaw is safe to try. The hot oven and the road need a grown-up first.

pool.prompt: You fall off your scooter. What now?
choices: Get up and have another go
Say scooters are not for you
pool.explain: Everyone falls when they learn to ride. Getting up and trying again is how you get better.

pool.prompt: Ella's frame has 5 steps. She climbed {n} steps, then took a big breath. How many steps are left to climb?
pool.hint: Count on from {n} up to 5, one step at a time.
pool.explain: From {n} up to 5 is {=5-n} steps. A breath, then one step at a time.
